chapter11_verse47.introduction: Bhagavad Gita Chapter 11 Verse 47 is situated within the sacred unfolding of the Bhagavad Gita, where narrative history and spiritual instruction are presented as living dharma rather than distant mythology. The scene arises amid complex human relationships, duties to family and kingdom, and the tension between personal emotion and cosmic order. Elders, seekers, warriors, and sages become participants in a moral universe in which every action carries both visible and subtle consequences. The traditional telling preserves memory of lineage, vows, pilgrimage spaces, and divine intervention, allowing the listener to see how Sanatana Dharma is practiced in difficult circumstances rather than in abstraction alone. This section should be approached as both sacred literature and ethical guidance: it teaches how intention, discipline, and reverence shape conduct. The narrative focus here is a precise spiritual instruction delivered in the battlefield dialogue of Kurukṣetra. By reflecting on character motives, setting, and dialogue, the reader enters the contemplative method of itihasa study, where historical remembrance supports inner refinement and devotion.

verse.sanskrit:
श्रीभगवानुवाच |
मया प्रसन्नेन तवार्जुनेदं
रूपं परं दर्शितमात्मयोगात् |
तेजोमयं विश्वमनन्तमाद्यं
यन्मे त्वदन्येन न दृष्टपूर्वम् ||११-४७||
verse.transliteration:
śrībhagavānuvāca .
mayā prasannena tavārjunedaṃ rūpaṃ paraṃ darśitamātmayogāt .
tejomayaṃ viśvamanantamādyaṃ yanme tvadanyena na dṛṣṭapūrvam ||11-47||
verse.translation: 11.47 The Blessed Lord said  O Arjuna, this Cosmic Form has graciously been shown to thee by Me by My own Yogic power; full of splendour, primeval, and infinite, this Cosmic Form of Mine has never been seen before by anyone other than thyself.

chapter11_verse47.philosophical_explanation: Bhagavad Gita Chapter 11 Verse 47 offers a layered teaching on disciplined action, inner clarity, and God-centered wisdom, presenting dharma as a harmonizing principle that integrates duty, knowledge, devotion, and self-mastery. In Vedantic reflection, the outer event is never merely external; it mirrors the inner field of the seeker where attachment, fear, pride, compassion, and discernment contend for dominance. The text therefore asks the reader to cultivate viveka, sustained discrimination between the permanent and the impermanent, while remaining active in righteous responsibilities. It also emphasizes that true strength is not aggression but alignment with satya, ahimsa in intent, self-restraint, and surrender to the Divine will. Ethical life in Sanatana Dharma emerges through disciplined action offered without egoic possessiveness, where one performs svadharma with humility and accountability. This teaching is socially relevant because it links personal transformation with collective order: families, communities, and governance remain stable only when conduct is rooted in justice, gratitude, and reverence for truth. Spiritually, the section invites bhakti and contemplative awareness, showing that liberation-oriented living can begin within ordinary duties when the heart is purified through right understanding and service.
